## Simple explanation

Generative AI refers to systems that create content, such as a written
response, image, audio clip, or code, in response to an input or prompt.

## Technical explanation

Generative systems learn patterns in data and model a distribution or
conditional distribution from which outputs can be produced. Approaches
include autoregressive models, diffusion models, variational
autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks. Generation does not
guarantee truth, originality, or usefulness.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Generative models support assistants, creative tools, summarization,
code generation, and synthetic media. Building useful applications
requires evaluation, data and licensing review, safeguards, and
integration with reliable tools or sources where appropriate.

## How it works

A model is trained on examples using an objective suited to its
architecture. At inference, it conditions on an input and produces an
output, often through iterative denoising or sequential token
prediction. Application systems may add retrieval, validation, and
human review.

## Practical example

A language model can draft a summary from a document. The application
can include citations or require a human to review the summary before
it is used in a high-impact decision.

## Common misconceptions

- Generative AI is not limited to chatbots or text.
- Fluent or realistic output is not necessarily accurate.
- A generated response is not automatically independent of patterns or
  material in training data.
